strengths: The core idea—using the same base MLLM as generator, principle-guided scorer/critic, and prompt refiner in a closed self-reflection loop to build preference data without human annotation or a stronger teacher—is a genuinely useful and relatively novel angle for the video detailed captioning literature, which has mostly relied on either human-curated scorers or distillation from larger proprietary/open models.

The curriculum DPO idea of ordering preference pairs by the score gap Δs (large-to-small) is simple, cheap to implement, and shown empirically to outperform vanilla DPO and SFT-only baselines by a clear margin (Tab. 3), giving a concrete, reusable training recipe.

Results on the VDC benchmark are strong relative to same-scale competitors: +5.13% accuracy / +0.27 score over the Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct base, and the method beats several methods that do use external teacher models (AVC-DPO, OwlCap, VideoCap-R1), which is a meaningful practical result given the reduced supervision requirement.

The ablation suite is reasonably thorough for a single-benchmark paper: self-reflection component ablation with inference-time cost reporting (Tab. 2), curriculum vs vanilla DPO vs SFT (Tab. 3), robustness to different human-written principle sets (Tab. 4), and sensitivity to max iterations T with compute-cost tradeoff (Tab. 5). This gives readers a fairly complete picture of what drives the gains and the sensitivity of the method to design choices.

The paper is clearly written, the pipeline is described with reasonably precise notation (Eq. 1-3), and the qualitative example in Fig. 3 supports the quantitative claims with a concrete illustration of reduced hallucination and richer detail capture.
weaknesses: All results are reported on a single benchmark (VDC) with a single backbone (Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct); there is no evaluation on other video captioning benchmarks (e.g., Shot2Story, VATEX, or downstream tasks like text-to-video generation or retrieval) to demonstrate generality of the learned captioner beyond the specific VDCscore metric that the training pipeline itself is implicitly optimizing toward (the principles and scorer plausibly overlap conceptually with what VDCscore measures), raising a risk of benchmark-specific overfitting rather than general captioning improvement.

The scoring/suggestion module and the base captioner share the same backbone and weights (self-scoring), which raises a fundamental soundness concern: since no external verifier or ground truth is used, the whole self-improvement loop’s ceiling is bounded by the model’s own blind spots and biases — a model that hallucinates or misjudges quality could reinforce its own errors. The paper does not analyze or discuss this risk (e.g., no analysis of scorer calibration/reliability, no correlation between the internal score and human judgment or the final VDCscore metric).

The maximum-iteration ablation (Tab. 5) shows continued modest improvement even at T=6, suggesting the method has not clearly saturated and T=4 seems chosen mainly for compute-cost reasons rather than being demonstrated as an optimal stopping point; the generation-time costs reported (hundreds of GPU-hours for a 4K-video corpus) suggest limited scalability to larger unlabeled corpora, which somewhat undercuts the “no expensive teacher needed” framing since the self-reflection loop itself is compute-heavy.

The comparison table includes only ~7B-scale models; there is no experiment scaling to larger backbones (the paper explicitly defers this to future work), so it remains unclear whether the self-reflection benefits diminish or persist at larger scale, limiting the demonstrated generality of the claimed contribution.

The dataset construction only uses 4,008 videos from a single corpus (Cockatiel-4K/OpenVid-1M), and captions are generated across only 5 fixed task dimensions defined by a prior taxonomy (from AuroraCap), which limits diversity of training signal and reduces the independence of this contribution from prior benchmark design choices.

The robustness-to-principles ablation (Tab. 4) is a nice check but only varies principle wording, not whether the principles/scorer are reliable evaluators of caption quality in an absolute sense (i.e., no correlation study between VDC-Agent's internal scores and either human ratings or the final benchmark's official scoring), so the core claim that self-assessment scores are meaningful is not directly validated.

strengths: The core idea of using a self-reflective agentic loop (caption generation, principle-guided scoring, prompt refinement, and reflection-on-failure) to construct preference data without human annotation or a larger teacher model is a reasonable and practically appealing direction for reducing annotation/API costs in video detailed captioning.
The curriculum DPO formulation that leverages the score gap Δs as a natural difficulty signal is a simple, low-overhead modification to standard DPO that is intuitive and easy to reproduce.

The paper provides a reasonably thorough set of ablations (self-reflection vs. principle-only vs. test-time reflection, SFT vs. vanilla DPO vs. curriculum DPO, robustness to principle wording, effect of max iterations T), which is helpful for understanding which components contribute to the gains.

Reported results show consistent improvement over the Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct baseline across all five VDC dimensions, and the method attains competitive numbers relative to several specialized captioners without using external teacher models or human labels, which is a meaningful practical advantage if the claims hold.
weaknesses: The 'self-improvement without external models' framing is somewhat overstated: the same base MLLM is used both as captioner and as the scorer/judge of its own captions. Self-scoring is known to be unreliable (models tend to overrate their own fluent but hallucinated outputs), and the paper provides no validation of the scoring function's correlation with human judgment or an independent metric. Since the entire preference dataset hinges on this self-assigned score, this is a central soundness gap.

The improvement over the base model (+5.13% accuracy, +0.27 score) is modest and is only evaluated on a single benchmark (VDC) that shares the same five-dimension taxonomy/scoring rubric the agent itself optimizes against; this raises a circularity concern where the pipeline may be tailored to the evaluation protocol rather than demonstrating general captioning improvement.
No statistical significance testing or variance across runs/seeds is reported, so it is unclear whether the modest absolute gains are robust.
Only a single base model scale (7B) is evaluated; claims about scalability to larger backbones are left to 'future work' and are not substantiated in the current submission.

Several baselines in Table 1 use human annotations or stronger external teacher models (e.g., AVC-DPO, VideoCap-R1, OwlCap); although flagged in the table, the paper's 'state-of-the-art' framing is only achieved via averaging, while on some dimensions (e.g., Short, Camera/Score) the resource-advantaged AVC-DPO still wins, which is not sufficiently discussed.

The comparison between test-time self-reflection (Baseline+P+R, 47.10/2.38) and the distilled trained model (49.08/2.50) shows the distilled model actually outperforming direct test-time reflection, but the paper does not provide a deeper analysis of why training-time distillation surpasses explicit test-time reasoning; this is left largely unexplained beyond a general claim of 'robustness and efficiency'.

Only the best/worst caption in each trajectory is kept to form preference pairs, discarding intermediate trajectory information; no comparison to alternative pair-selection strategies (e.g., adjacent-step pairs, all pairwise combinations) is provided to justify this design choice.
Reproducibility depends heavily on prompt/principle design and the self-scoring rubric, and it is unclear whether code, prompts, and the constructed VDC-Agent-19K dataset will be released.

The qualitative analysis is limited to a single cherry-picked example (Fig. 3); no broader failure-case analysis is presented to show whether the trained model introduces new hallucinations or biases amplified through iterative self-training on self-assigned scores.

strengths: Novel and practically appealing framework: VDC-Agent enables self-improvement of an MLLM captioner using only unlabeled videos, avoiding costly human annotation or reliance on larger/proprietary teacher models, which is a meaningful step toward more scalable and reproducible caption-data construction.

The closed-loop design (caption generation, principle-guided scoring/suggestion, prompt refinement, and self-reflection on regression) is clearly formalized (Eqs. 1-3) and intuitive, and the resulting curriculum DPO scheme that exploits the score gap Δs as a natural difficulty signal is a sensible and lightweight extension of standard DPO.

Strong empirical results: VDC-Agent-7B achieves state-of-the-art average accuracy/score on the VDC benchmark, outperforming several specialized captioners (including some that use external teacher models or human annotation), while keeping inference cost identical to the base model since the reflection is distilled into training rather than performed at test time.

The ablation studies are reasonably thorough: they isolate the contribution of principles vs. self-reflection vs. curriculum DPO (Tables 2-3), test sensitivity to different human-written principle sets (Table 4), and study the effect of the maximum iteration budget T with explicit compute-quality trade-off numbers (Table 5), which strengthens confidence that gains are not due to a single confound.
Qualitative example (Fig. 3) is illustrative and supports the claim that the model captures finer camera/background/interaction details than baselines with less hallucination.
weaknesses: The scoring and preference-pair construction rely entirely on the same base MLLM judging its own captions, with no external or human verification that the assigned scores correlate with actual caption quality; this raises a self-referential/self-preference bias concern (the model could be rewarded for traits it already over-produces, e.g., verbosity or specific phrasing patterns, rather than true faithfulness), which the paper does not empirically probe (e.g., via human agreement study with the automatic scorer).

Evaluation is confined to a single benchmark (VDC) and a single training video source (Cockatiel-4K, ~4K videos); there is no evaluation on other captioning benchmarks or downstream tasks (e.g., retrieval, VQA) to demonstrate that the learned captioning improvements generalize beyond this specific benchmark/metric.

Only one base model scale (Qwen2.5-VL-7B) is evaluated; the claim of a generally applicable self-evolving framework would be more convincing with at least one additional backbone or scale, especially since the future-work section explicitly flags this as untested.

No human evaluation of the final captions' quality/faithfulness is reported; all quantitative claims rest on the automatic VDCscore metric, which itself is computed by an MLLM judge, making the overall evaluation pipeline fully automatic end-to-end and potentially susceptible to shared biases between the training-time scorer and the evaluation-time scorer.

The reported gains, while state-of-the-art on average, are modest on the "short" dimension and closely matched or slightly below AVC-DPO on "camera" accuracy despite AVC-DPO using an external 72B teacher; a more detailed discussion of when/why the self-reflective approach under- or over-performs teacher-based approaches would strengthen the significance claims.

The data-generation process is computationally non-trivial (e.g., ~394 GPU-hours for T=4 in Table 5), which is not clearly contextualized against the cost savings claimed relative to teacher-based or human-annotation pipelines; a direct cost comparison would better support the paper's efficiency narrative.

The rule-based filtering step (discarding videos that reach the score threshold in one iteration) could bias the training set toward harder/atypical videos and away from cases the base model already handles well, but the potential effect of this selection bias on the final model's behavior is not analyzed.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated problem: existing VDC methods depend on costly human annotation or distillation from large proprietary/open teacher models; the paper proposes a genuinely external-supervision-free alternative via agentic self-reflection.

The overall pipeline (agentic generation/scoring/reflection -> preference dataset construction -> curriculum DPO internalization) is coherent and clearly described with formal notation and a clear system diagram.

Extensive empirical validation: SOTA results on VDC and DREAM-1K benchmarks, applied to three different base MLLMs (LLaVA-OneVision, InternVL2.5, Qwen2.5-VL) showing consistent, non-trivial gains, suggesting the method is not overfit to one backbone.

Thoughtful ablations: curriculum vs. random vs. anti-curriculum ordering, robustness to different independently written principle sets (including an industry standard from Shutterstock), sensitivity to max iteration T, and a compute-normalized comparison against Best-of-N sampling that helps rule out the trivial explanation that gains come merely from extra test-time compute.

Human evaluation (three independent annotators) and an AI judge (with position-bias control) are used to validate that the self-scored preference pairs actually align with human quality judgments, and a length-distribution analysis addresses the concern that preference is driven by caption length rather than content.

The internalization strategy is practically valuable: it recovers most of the benefit of iterative test-time reflection while keeping inference cost at the level of the base model, which is an important applied contribution for deployment.
weaknesses: Circularity/self-scoring risk: the same base MLLM serves as generator, scorer, and prompt-refiner without any external grounding signal (e.g., no verification against actual video content beyond the model's own judgment), so systematic biases or blind spots of the base model could be reinforced rather than corrected; the human-evaluation check is only on 500 sampled pairs, which does not fully rule out reward-hacking behavior (e.g., stylistic patterns preferred by the self-scorer but not strongly tied to factual accuracy).

The training corpus for dataset construction (Cockatiel-4K, ~4,008 videos) is relatively small and drawn from a single source (OpenVid-1M); scalability and generalization of the self-reflection agent to more diverse or longer video domains is not demonstrated.

The paper does not report the total compute/API cost of running the iterative agentic pipeline itself (multiple MLLM calls per video across 5 dimensions and up to T=4 iterations, generating 20,040 raw trajectories) in comparison to the cost of simply using an external stronger teacher model once; while inference-time efficiency is well argued, the offline data-generation cost trade-off vs. distillation methods is under-analyzed.

Some comparison choices are unusual: baselines include models such as "GPT-5.4" and "Gemini 3.1 Pro" that are unlikely to exist as of the claimed evaluation period, raising concerns about the provenance/verifiability of these comparison numbers and general result reproducibility for these entries.

Hyperparameter choices (e.g., score threshold λ=90, LoRA rank/alpha, T=4 default) are reported but not extensively justified via sensitivity analysis beyond the iteration-count ablation; broader robustness of the curriculum DPO recipe to different β or dataset scales is not explored.

No discussion of failure cases where self-reflection degrades performance or fails to converge, nor detailed statistics on self-reflection trigger rate/effectiveness in the main text (deferred to appendix), limiting insight into the mechanism's actual behavior distribution.

strengths: Addresses a practically important problem: removing dependency on human annotation or large external teacher models for video detailed captioning, which is a legitimate and under-explored direction.
Extensive experimental section: cross-model generalization is shown on three different base MLLMs (LLaVA-OneVision, InternVL2.5, Qwen2.5-VL), consistent gains on both VDC and DREAM-1K benchmarks.

Thoughtful set of ablations, including robustness to different principle sets (even an industrial Shutterstock-derived set), sensitivity to the max iteration count T, and a compute-normalized comparison against Best-of-N sampling that helps rule out the trivial explanation that gains come purely from extra test-time compute.

The curriculum DPO idea of using the agent's own score gap as a difficulty signal for ordering preference pairs is a sensible and relatively simple design, and the ablation against random/anti-curriculum ordering supports its usefulness.

Human evaluation (3 annotators) plus an independent LLM judge with order-swap control is used to validate that the self-generated preference pairs align with human quality judgments, and a length-bias check is included to rule out a trivial length confound.

The internalization strategy (distilling iterative self-reflection into a single forward pass via DPO) is a reasonable and practically motivated solution to the latency problem of iterative agentic refinement, and the ablation (Table 4) clearly demonstrates the efficiency/accuracy trade-off it resolves.
weaknesses: Core self-evolution loop is self-referential: the same backbone model that generates captions also scores/critiques them and supplies the preference signal used to update itself. While the 500-pair human/GPT-judge study offers some reassurance that y+ is generally preferred over y-, this is a validation of the data construction pairs, not of the final fine-tuned model's outputs versus baselines, leaving the risk of the model learning to exploit the self-scorer's idiosyncrasies (reward hacking) insufficiently examined.

Many essential reproducibility details — the exact principles R, the full algorithmic pseudocode, self-reflection trigger-rate statistics, and prompt templates for scoring/refinement/reflection — are deferred entirely to the (unavailable) Appendix, making it difficult to fully assess soundness and reproducibility from the main text alone.

No variance/multiple-seed results are reported for the DPO training or the agentic data generation process; given the sensitivity of LLM fine-tuning and the fairly modest absolute gaps in some ablations (e.g., anti-curriculum vs. random DPO), the significance of several reported differences is unclear.

Experiments are confined to ~7-8B backbones; the promised scaling to larger models (e.g., Qwen-32B) is left to future work, so claims about general applicability of the framework to different model scales are not yet substantiated.

The technical novelty is largely a combination of existing ideas (self-refine/self-reward style iterative critique, DPO, curriculum learning for preference pairs) rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic contribution; the curriculum-DPO ordering strategy itself is a direct application of prior curriculum-learning-for-preference-optimization work cited in the paper.

Dataset construction, while framed as removing dependency on external supervision, still requires a non-trivial compute budget (tens of GPU-hours to build the ~19K preference pairs from only ~4K source videos), and this cost/scalability trade-off versus simply using a stronger teacher model is not discussed quantitatively.

Some table entries (e.g., SynPO row in Table 1 with missing Accuracy values, and the comparison baselines including very recent/large proprietary models) make the comparison table a bit uneven, and the comparison against general MLLMs with very different parameter counts and training budgets is not fully controlled for.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and well-motivated problem: existing VDC methods depend on costly human annotation or larger teacher models; the proposed self-reflection loop removes this dependency, which is a meaningful practical contribution.

The 'internalization' idea (distilling iterative self-reflection into a single forward pass via curriculum DPO) directly targets and convincingly solves the latency problem that plagues most agentic/test-time-refinement methods, and the compute-normalized comparison against Best-of-N (Table 8) makes a compelling case that the gains come from directed reasoning rather than simply more sampling.

Extensive and well-designed ablations: curriculum vs. random vs. anti-curriculum ordering (Table 5), sensitivity to principle wording using four independently authored principle sets including an industrial standard (Table 6), and the effect of maximum iteration depth T (Table 7), all of which support the robustness of the design choices.

Demonstrated generalization across three different base MLLMs (LLaVA-OneVision, InternVL2.5, Qwen2.5-VL) with consistent gains on both VDC and DREAM-1K benchmarks, suggesting the framework is largely method-agnostic rather than tailored to one backbone.

Human evaluation (Table 3) and a length-bias analysis (Fig. 3) directly address the natural concern that self-generated/self-scored preference pairs may be unreliable or merely reward verbosity, strengthening the credibility of the constructed VDC-Agent-19K dataset.
Clear qualitative example illustrating that the method reduces hallucination and captures finer-grained details (camera motion, spatial layout) compared to strong baselines.
weaknesses: The self-reflection/scoring mechanism uses the same base MLLM (or a model sharing its backbone) to judge its own captions; this self-evaluation is fundamentally bounded by the base model's own perceptual blind spots, so systematic hallucinations or missed details that the model cannot itself detect are unlikely to be corrected—this limitation is not explicitly discussed despite being central to the method's soundness.

Dataset construction is itself computationally expensive (up to ~49–72 GPU-hours on 8×A800 for T=4–6 per the reported dataset-construction times), so while inference is efficient, the overall pipeline cost relative to alternative distillation-based approaches is not clearly contextualized.

Several core implementation details (principle text, exact system prompts for the reflection/refiner modules, self-reflection trigger rate, pseudo-code) are deferred entirely to the Appendix, which is not included here, making it harder to fully judge reproducibility and the precise mechanics of the reflection trigger from the main text alone.

Only the best/worst captions from each trajectory are used to form DPO pairs, discarding intermediate iterations; the paper does not explore or justify alternative pair-construction strategies (e.g., adjacent-step pairs) that might further inform whether the curriculum signal is optimally extracted.

The technical novelty is somewhat incremental: it largely combines known ideas (LLM self-refinement/reflection agents such as Reflexion/Self-Refine, and curriculum learning applied to DPO) and applies them to the VDC domain, rather than introducing fundamentally new algorithmic mechanisms.

Gains are noticeably smaller on the 'Short' summarization dimension, and the paper does not deeply analyze whether the framework's benefits are primarily about adding more (correct) detail versus improving core semantic/temporal understanding beyond what length/detail-oriented metrics capture.
